readings.c2s1:
¶
'''Yule''' (yöl), ''v. i.''; pret. and pp. ''Yuled'', ppr. ''Yuling''. [< ''Yule'', ''n.''] To celebrate Yule or Christmas. ''Halliwell''; ''Jamieson''. [Prov. Eng. and Scotch.]

'''Yule-tide''' (yöl′tīd), ''n.'' The time or season of Yule or Christmas.
{{smaller block|In the old clog almanacs, a wheel is the device employed for marking the season of ''Yule-tide''.
{{right|''Chambers’s Book of Days'', II. 746.}}}}

'''Yuncinæ''' (yun-sī′nē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., prop. ''Iynginæ''; < ''Yunx'', prop. ''Iynx'' (''Iyng-''), + ''-inæ''.] Same as ''Iynginæ''. ''G. R. Gray'', 1840.

'''yungan''' (yung′gan), ''n.'' [Native name.] The dugong. ''E. P. Wright.''

'''Yungidæ, Yunginæ,''' ''n. pl.'' Same as ''Iyngidæ'', ''Iynginæ''.

'''Yunx''' (yungks), ''n.'' [NL. (Linnæus, 1766 or earlier), also ''Jynx'' and ''Iynx'', < Gr. ἴυγξ, the wryneck.] '''1.''' Same as ''Iynx''.—'''2.''' [''l. c.''] The wryneck, ''Iynx torquilla''. See cut under ''wryneck''.
{{smaller block|The ''Yunx'', a genuine Woodpecker, hath a tail as long in proportion to his body, and marked with crosse-bars too.
{{right|''John Ray'', in Ellis’s Lit. Letters, p. 200.}}}}

'''yupon''' (yö′pọn), ''n.'' Same as ''yapon.'' ''Sportsman’s Gazetteer.''

'''yure''' (yör), ''n.'' See ''ewer''<sup>3</sup>. [Prov. Eng.]

'''yurt''' (yört), ''n.'' [Siberian.] One of the houses or huts, whether permanent or movable, of the natives of northern and central Asia. Also ''yourta'', ''yourte'', ''jurt.''
{{smaller block|It [the lake] is ten miles in circumference, and here and there are ''yourtes'' inhabited by the Mongols.
{{right|''Huc'', Travels (trans. 1852), I. 206.}}}}

'''yutu''' (yö′tö), ''n.'' [Peruv.] A species of tinamou, found in Peru.
{{smaller block|A partridge called ''yutu'' frequents the long grass.
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', XVIII. 673.}}}}

'''yux†''', ''v.'' and ''n.'' An obsolete variant of ''yex.''

'''yve†''', ''n.'' An old spelling of ''ivy''<sup>1</sup>.

'''yvel†''', ''a.'', ''n.'', and ''adv.'' An old spelling of ''evil''<sup>1</sup>.

'''yvoire†''', '''yvory†'''. Old spellings of ''ivory''<sup>1</sup>.

'''ywis†''', ''adv.'' and ''n.'' See ''iwis.''

'''ywrake†'''. An obsolete preterit of ''wreak''<sup>1</sup>.

'''ywrie†'''. An obsolete past participle of ''wry''<sup>2</sup>.

'''ywroke†'''. An obsolete preterit of ''wreak''<sup>1</sup>.

'''yye†''', ''n.'' A Middle English form of ''eye''<sup>1</sup>.

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|Yule|7027|yye}}</noinclude>{{nop}}{{smaller block|An enormous log glowing and blazing, and sending forth a vast volume of light and heat, . . . was the ''Yule clog'', which the squire was particular in having brought in and illumined on a Christmas eve, according to ancient custom.
{{right|''Irving'', Sketch-Book, p. 247.}}}}

'''Yule cake.''' Same as ''Yule dough.''   ''Hone'', Every-Day Book, I. 1638.—'''Yule candle,''' a large candle used for light during the festivities of Christmas eve. In many places the exhaustion of the candle before the end of the evening was believed to portend ill luck, and any piece remaining was carefully preserved to be burnt out at the owner’s like-wake.
{{smaller block|As an accompaniment to the Yule log, a candle of monstrous size, called the ''Yule candle'', or Christmas candle, shed its light on the festive-board during the evening.
{{right|''Chambers’s Book of Days'', II. 735.}}}}

'''Yule dough''' (dialectal ''doo, dow''), a cake made especially for Christmas time. Also called ''baby-cake'' (because representing in shape a baby, probably the infant Christ) and ''Yule cake.''
{{smaller block|The ''Yule-Dough'' (or ''Dow''), a Kind of Baby or little Image of Paste, which our Bakers used formerly to bake at this Season, and present to their Customers, in the same Manner as the Chandlers gave Christmas Candles.
{{right|''Bourne’s Pop. Antiq.'' (1777), p. 163.}}}}

{{smaller block|In the north of England the common people still make a sort of little images at Christmas, which they call ''Yule Doos.''
{{right|''The Listener'' (1836), I. 62 (quoted in N. and Q., [7th ser., XI. 6).}}}}
